n: When Mordecai learns of the decree, he tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth and ashes, and walks through the city crying out loudly. His public grief is also a public protest.

f.g: Rough mourning garments and ashes on the head — signs of deep grief and humility.

f.w: a loud and a bitter cry

n: He goes as far as the palace gate, but no one in mourning clothes was allowed inside the king’s presence. The royal court kept sorrow out of sight.
Across the empire, Jews mourn, fast, weep, and wail. Though God is never named in Esther, fasting implies prayer to Him.
Esther hears that Mordecai is in mourning and sends fresh clothes, but he refuses them. She doesn’t yet know about the decree — palace life had isolated her.

f.g: He refused, because his mourning was meant to be seen.

n: She sends Hatach, a trusted attendant, to find out what is wrong.

f.g: A eunuch assigned to serve the queen, acting as messenger.

n: Hatach meets Mordecai in the city square outside the palace gate.
Mordecai explains everything, even the exact amount of money Haman promised. He has done his research.
He gives Hatach a copy of the decree for Esther to read and urges her to go to the king and plead for her people. It is the first time Esther is asked to reveal who she is.

f.g: Openly identifying herself as a Jew.

n: Hatach reports Mordecai’s message to Esther.
Esther sends back her reply through Hatach.

She explains the danger: anyone who approaches the king uninvited faces death unless he holds out his golden scepter. And the king hasn’t called for her in a month — perhaps a sign she had lost favor.

f.g: The royal staff; extending it granted mercy and permission to speak.

n: Esther’s words are relayed to Mordecai.
Mordecai’s answer is firm: don’t imagine that living in the palace will save you. Your secret will not protect you forever.

This is the key verse of the book. If Esther stays silent, deliverance will come from somewhere else — Mordecai trusts that God will save His people — but she will miss her role. Perhaps she became queen for exactly this moment. God places people where they can serve.

f.g: Many readers see a quiet reference to God, who is never named in Esther.

f.w: for such a time as this

n: She asks all the Jews in Susa to fast for her for three days, and she and her maids will fast too. Then she will go to the king against the law. “If I perish, I perish” — a courageous surrender of her life to God’s will.
Now Mordecai obeys Esther. The roles have reversed — the young woman he raised is now leading.

f.w: did according to all that Esther had commanded him
